title: "Structure"
subtitle: "Minutes 13–23. From raw OCR to a hybrid workflow, developed with Claude Code."

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Terms on this page"}
- **JSON**: a plain-text format for a record: named fields in braces, lists in brackets (see the glossary for Trimen's).
- **prompt**: the written instructions sent to the model with each entry.
- **regex grammar**: pattern rules that match text by its shape, written in Python; the deterministic first tier.
- **validator**: Python that checks every place and year the model wrote against the source and drops what is not there.
- **post-normaliser**: Python that applies the systematic fixes found by the audit, logging each change.
- **vLLM**: an open-source server that runs an open model on a GPU and answers like a commercial API.
- **GPU**: the graphics card the model runs on; the model has to fit in its memory.
- **token**: the unit a model reads and writes in, roughly three-quarters of a word.
- **reasoning mode**: a setting where the model writes out its thinking before answering; off here, because it spent the budget and returned nothing.
- **frontier model / open model**: frontier refers to leading capability; open refers here to downloadable model weights. These are different properties, not opposites. The project used a commercial coding agent and an open model inside the pipeline.
- **deterministic**: done by fixed rules, so the same input always gives the same output; no model involved.

All terms: [glossary](../glossary.qmd).
:::

## Start by showing Claude Code the raw OCR

I began by showing Claude Code the raw OCR and discussing whether Python could structure it on its own. We read examples, discussed what a record should contain, and worked out where explicit rules would be reliable and where the text needed interpretation.

Balmer’s original OCR block, before abbreviation expansion:

> BALMER, F. E.—Dep. chief acctnt., G.P.O., E. Africa Prot., Mar., 1919; ch. acctnt., G.P.O., Kenya, Oct., 1919; ch. acctnt., Kenya-Uganda-Tanganyika post and tel. service, 1933; senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935.

The [saved raw block](../outputs/structure/balmer-raw-ocr.json) retains its bounding box and source location: the 1936 volume, printed page 614, OCR page index 832, block index 11. The OCR page index and printed page number differ.

For a similar discussion with your coding agent, start with:

> Read this OCR sample. What could Python extract reliably using explicit rules? Show the clauses those rules would struggle with. Propose fields and two example records, then explain how Python and a model could share the work.

## Why regular expressions alone were insufficient

This is a familiar problem for historians: **semi-structured data**. Names, offices, places and dates recur, but their relationships are expressed in varied prose. The irregularity belongs to the source as well as to the OCR.

| Example | What a reading must establish |
|---|---|
| Balmer: “senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935” | The new position inherits the preceding place |
| Blakely: “B. Honduras, Apl., 1898” | “B.” abbreviates British Honduras; April 1898 dates the appointment |
| Trimen: lecturer, 1867–1875; British Museum assistant, 1869–1879 | Two appointments overlap; one does not end when the other begins |

A regular expression can recognise a year or a specified abbreviation. Binding that year to the correct posting, carrying a place across an omitted phrase, or separating concurrent jobs needs more context. A fixed grammar could handle the regular cases, but adding exceptions did not make it a reliable parser for the whole collection.

Python remained useful for splitting the input, parsing regular clauses, managing the run and checking outputs. We developed a hybrid so a model could read the difficult clauses within an agreed structure.

## Develop and check the hybrid

The collaboration with Claude Code produced the schema, Python stages and extraction prompt. We settled the fields on a sample, inspected example records against their source, and revised the rules. The [in-session runbook](../outputs/structure/structuring-loop-runbook.md) records batches of reference examples followed by Python validation. The model inside the eventual batch script was Qwen; Claude Code was the environment used to develop the machinery.

The resulting workflow had three parts. It ran for the Colonial Office List in June 2026 and for the India Office List a week later:

1. **Python first.** A regex grammar for the printed entry shape parses what it can. It is all-or-nothing: if any clause containing a year fails to parse cleanly, the whole entry is refused rather than half-parsed. A second Python pass expands the abbreviations it recognises ("Feb." to "February", "acctnt." to "accountant") and leaves everything else exactly as printed.
2. **A model for what Python cannot do.** Binding position to place to time span across run-on, elided, "ditto" and concurrent clauses. One entry in, one JSON object out. For the Colonial Office List the first residue went to a batch API with a cheap commercial model; the bulk of both corpora went to an open model on a university GPU.
3. **Python again.** A validator that checks every place and year the model emitted against the source text and drops what it cannot find there. Then a post-normalisation pass that applies the deterministic fixes found by the audit, logging every change.

## The schema

One object per entry: `surname`, `given_names`, `birth_year` (only if printed), `education`, `honours` with award years, `events`, and `terminal`. One event per posting: `position` and `place` as printed, `year_start`, `year_end`, `place_inherited`, `is_acting`, and `civil` or `military`. The agent and the historian settled it on a sample before any batch ran.


The user message is the entry alone, after the abbreviation pass. Trimen's 1889 entry goes in like this ([file](../outputs/structure/extraction-user-message-example.txt)):

```{.text}
{{< include ../outputs/structure/extraction-user-message-example.txt >}}
```

Three things to notice. Every rule in the list exists because an earlier run broke it; the rule about birth years is there because a model had been inferring them from the first appointment. The last paragraph pins the key names, because a bake-off found the model drifting to `name` and `decoration` without it. And nothing in the prompt is about the historical question; it is entirely about what the page says and how to hold it.

## The overnight run

| | Colonial Office List | India Office List |
|---|---|---|
| Model | Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, served by vLLM on a university GPU box | same |
| Settings | temperature 0, reasoning off, 8 to 16 workers, 4 retries | same |
| Entries | 34,743 | 30,496 |
| Rate once warm | about 1 a second | 1.03 a second |
| Elapsed | about a day including setup, 19–20 June | 8.24 hours, overnight 25–26 June |
| Failed to return valid JSON | | 55, under 0.2 per cent |

The handoff note records the setting that matters most: reasoning off. With it on, long entries eat the token budget and return no JSON, a 67 per cent failure rate. Thinking off, temperature zero: the same finding every run on this corpus has made.

The India Office List needed one new piece of code, a Python segmenter for its different OCR format, written that morning. The prompt, the model, the validator and the post-normaliser were reused unchanged through one environment variable. The graph was published that afternoon.

## Two kinds of model

Claude in Claude Code structured about 200 entries in-session as the reference set and wrote the pipeline with the historian’s direction. The open model inside the script read the corpus. Every record says which path produced it. The runbook for the in-session loop is [saved](../outputs/structure/structuring-loop-runbook.md).

## What came back

Trimen's entry, structured ([saved](../outputs/structure/trimen-structured.json)):

| position | place | years | |
|---|---|---|---|
| lecturer on botany | London | 1867–1875 | |
| senior assistant to department of botany | British Museum | 1869–1879 | overlaps the first: two concurrent posts, two events |
| director Royal Botanical Gardens | Ceylon | 1880– | |

Plus `education: "M.B. (Lond.)"`, two honours without years, no birth year, no terminal event. In the published graph the first and third events are placed; "British Museum" is an institution, not a place, and stays unplaced.

## The audit

Structured records were read against their source by a reviewer model, in three rounds, and the findings categorised ([catalogue](../outputs/audit/struct-error-catalog.md), [round 1 pairs](../outputs/audit/every10-reviewed-pairs.json)). The figures are before the post-normaliser described below:

| Round | Sample | Fully clean | Major error |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | every tenth of the first 1,859 records: 186 | 129 (69%) | 6 records (3.2%); 8 findings |
| 2 | 100 spread across the corpus | 51 (51%) | 9 (about 9%) |
| 3 | 300 spread across the corpus | about 149 (50%) | not tallied |

Round 1 sampled only the first 1,859 records; it was not spread across the corpus. Rounds 2 and 3 cover a broader range. These are sample results, not a measured accuracy rate for the finished graph. A model did the reading in all three; the examples below were checked by hand.

Three of the findings, source beside record ([saved](../outputs/structure/audit-examples.json)):

**The ditto that was not resolved.** Balmer's last clause, "senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935", came back with `place: "do."`. The rule says inherit; the model copied the abbreviation.

**The appointment date that became a birth year.** "BLAKELY, DONALD QUENTIN.—Clk., atty.-gen.'s off., B. Honduras, Apl., 1898." came back with `birth_year: 1898` and an event with no year. The prompt forbids exactly this. The same record expanded "off." to "officer" instead of "office".

**The knighthood split in two.** "KT. BACH. (1920)" came back as two honours, `KT` and `BACH (1920)`. Three records in the sample did the same.

## Why the fix was not a bigger model

The errors are not random. They are a handful of systematic patterns: a short list of abbreviations mis-expanded the same way every time, ditto marks left literal, one compound honour split, "mentioned in despatches" dropped. Each has a deterministic fix, and those fixes are the post-normalisation pass: merge `KT` + `BACH` into Knight Bachelor; forward-fill a "do." place from the previous event and set the flag; strip honorifics folded into given names; "officer in chief" back to "officer in charge"; drop a military tag with no military signal in the position. Every change is appended to a list on the record, so nothing is silent. The "off." expansion is fixed one step earlier, by not pre-expanding ambiguous abbreviations at all.

The fixes do not establish the accuracy of the finished corpus. That needs a new audit after normalisation, including records changed by each rule and a fresh sample. A more capable model would also need that audit.

## One correction, checked

Here is a small replay you can run without a model or a network. It uses the three saved audit records above: twelve events in all. It changes only a literal “do.” or “ditto” when the preceding event has a resolved place.

| | Balmer’s fourth event |
|---|---|
| Source | “senr. dep. P.M.G., do., 1935” |
| Before | `place: "do."`, `place_inherited: true` |
| After | `place: "Kenya-Uganda-Tanganyika"`, `place_inherited: true` |
| Reason kept with the change | Printed ditto; the previous event supplies the place |

**Checked:** one event changed; the other eleven events and all other fields stayed unchanged. A second run made no further changes. Constructed boundary cases with no preceding resolved place stayed unresolved. Blakely’s birth-year error and Connolly’s split knighthood remain: this rule fixes one class of error.

[Saved before-and-after records and checks](../outputs/structure/ditto-fix-replay.json). To reproduce from the workshop repository:

```bash
python3 scripts/demo_ditto_fix.py
```

This is a workshop replay on three records, not a rerun of the published graph or a post-fix accuracy estimate.

**You decide:** what is an event. Whether an acting appointment is a posting. Whether "called to the bar, 1879" belongs in the career. Whether "leader of leg. coun. from 1906 to 1911" is a position or a description. The prompt records those decisions; the audit checks whether the model kept them; the post-normaliser enforces the ones that can be enforced.
